meta.title: Statistics backbone
meta.scope: A broad proposed map from mathematical preparation through undergraduate statistics and selected master's electives; not an exhaustive or official curriculum.
meta.stages: Foundation, U (undergraduate), M (master's), U–M and elective are approximate study bands, independent of hierarchy levels. Every master's program selects a subset.
meta.organization: Each concept has one display parent. Cross-links express prerequisites, applications or comparisons, not additional duplicate nodes. The three roots and exact hierarchy are an authored synthesis.
meta.evidence: Sources support topic coverage and study scope. Course/book-sized units and chapters are proposed groupings, not claims about the exact tables of contents. Cross-link explanations are authored conceptual synthesis, not a complete formal prerequisite graph.
meta.questions: Question-form leaves are suggested study prompts unless explicitly mapped to a supplied question. No learning mastery is inferred.
meta.obsidian: External planning artifact. No vault pages, settings, logs or digest checkpoints were edited.

nodes.label: Probability & mathematical foundations
nodes.description: The language and mathematical tools for describing randomness; mathematics here is a supporting foundation.

nodes.label: Mathematical tools
nodes.description: Calculus, geometry and proof tools used throughout statistical reasoning.

nodes.label: Probability foundations
nodes.description: Events, probability models and updating with information.

nodes.label: Random variables & distributions
nodes.description: Describe one quantity, its transformations and its average behavior.

nodes.label: Joint variation & conditioning
nodes.description: Build multivariate models and separate different meanings of dependence.

nodes.label: Independence versus zero covariance
nodes.description: Independence implies zero covariance when moments exist. The reverse needs additional structure, such as joint Gaussianity.

nodes.label: Limits & concentration
nodes.description: Connect random samples to stable averages and useful approximations.

nodes.label: Stochastic processes
nodes.description: Model sequences and indexed collections of random quantities.

nodes.label: Statistical inference & modeling
nodes.description: Learn about populations and mechanisms, quantify uncertainty, design studies and build interpretable models.

nodes.label: Inference foundations
nodes.description: What is being estimated, how data arise and what uncertainty means.

nodes.label: Frequentist & likelihood inference
nodes.description: Estimate and test using the sampling behavior of statistical procedures.

nodes.label: Bayesian inference
nodes.description: Update uncertain quantities with data and examine the resulting model.

nodes.label: Regression & linear models
nodes.description: Describe conditional responses, estimate effects and assess model assumptions.

nodes.label: Residual variance and degrees of freedom
One-restriction F equals t squared
nodes.description: For a single linear restriction in the same Gaussian linear model, the matching F statistic equals t squared; joint restrictions need not reduce to one t statistic.

nodes.label: R squared and adjusted R squared
Design, sampling & causality
nodes.description: Create informative data and separate design-based claims from model assumptions.

nodes.label: Nonparametric & robust inference
nodes.description: Relax distributional assumptions and examine sensitivity.

nodes.label: Multivariate analysis
nodes.description: Understand variation across several measured quantities.

nodes.label: Time series & forecasting
nodes.description: Analyze temporal dependence and predict future observations.

nodes.label: Event-time & reliability
nodes.description: Model time until an event while accounting for censoring and incomplete observation.

nodes.label: Spatial statistics
nodes.description: Model observations whose locations create dependence and guide prediction.

nodes.label: Applied statistics & evidence
nodes.description: Connect general methods to incomplete data, scientific domains and responsible practice.

nodes.label: Statistical computing & learning
nodes.description: Implement statistical reasoning, fit complex models and assess prediction reliably.

nodes.label: Programming, data & visualization
nodes.description: Turn raw data and statistical algorithms into trustworthy analyses.

nodes.label: Numerical methods & optimization
nodes.description: Compute stable estimates and solve statistical objectives.

nodes.label: Simulation & approximate inference
nodes.description: Approximate integrals, sampling distributions and posterior quantities.

nodes.label: Monte Carlo error versus posterior uncertainty
Variational inference
nodes.description: Approximate a posterior through optimization. ELBO derivations link this chapter to probability, Bayesian inference and optimization.

nodes.label: Calculate the ELBO
nodes.description: For observed x, latent z and a trial density q, assemble expected log joint minus expected log q. The posterior-KL identity and Jensen give the same bound under suitable support and finiteness conditions.

nodes.label: Why do Jensen and KL give the same bound?
Statistical learning & prediction
nodes.description: Learn predictive rules and judge performance on appropriate unseen data.

nodes.label: Prediction uncertainty
nodes.description: Elective introduction. Standard split conformal provides marginal coverage under exchangeability, not arbitrary conditional coverage or protection from distribution shift.

nodes.label: Probabilistic models & neural methods
nodes.description: Selected master's-level introductions linking latent variables, probability and learning.

edges.reason: Probability supplies sampling models; inference reasons from observed data about their unknown features.
Statistical models define objectives and uncertainty; computation fits and checks the procedures.
Simulation implements probability models and uses probabilistic error analysis.
OLS fits the projection of the response onto the design column space.
Eigenvectors and singular values describe principal directions of variation.
Stable matrix algorithms implement linear-algebra operations in statistical fitting.
Taylor linearization transfers a limiting distribution through a smooth function.
Integration and Jacobians transform density-weighted probability regions.
Convexity gives useful global optimality conditions for statistical objectives.
Concavity of log bounds the log of an expectation; support and integrability conditions matter.
The ELBO gap is KL from the variational distribution to the posterior when the identity is well-defined.
Bayes rule updates the prior using the likelihood and its normalizing evidence.
Causal identification adds assumptions linking observational conditionals to interventions.
An estimator is a random variable or vector because its input sample is random.
Exact normal-sample laws provide t, chi-square and F reference distributions.
The conditional mean minimizes square loss; OLS restricts prediction to a linear class.
Conditional expected loss determines optimal actions for a given loss.
Total variance distinguishes within-resample variation from variation across original datasets.
Hierarchical predictions average over latent parameters and groups.
Gaussian errors yield exact normal coefficient laws and independent residual quadratic forms.
Linear Gaussian conditioning is the update behind the Kalman filter.
Graphical models encode particular conditional-independence statements.
Sample averages provide elementary consistent estimators when LLN conditions hold.
Asymptotic normal inference combines suitable CLTs with estimator-specific arguments.
Replacing a population scale by a consistent estimate supports asymptotic pivots.
Delta-method uncertainty yields approximate intervals for transformed parameters.
Monte Carlo averages converge under applicable LLN conditions.
A suitable CLT supplies a Monte Carlo error approximation.
Finite-sample bounds help control deviations between empirical and population quantities.
MCMC constructs a Markov chain with the desired invariant distribution.
Having an invariant target alone does not establish that a finite simulation has mixed.
Arrival times supply elementary examples of survival and hazard modeling.
Covariance kernels describe correlated random fields for spatial prediction.
Forecast innovations connect conditional-mean reasoning to dynamic modeling.
A precise estimand and population are needed before selecting an analysis.
Bootstrap simulation approximates how a statistic varies across samples.
Bias–variance decompositions relate estimation error to predictive risk; prediction can add outcome noise.
GLMs use an exponential-family likelihood and a link for the conditional mean.
Event-time inference must incorporate censoring or use an appropriate partial likelihood.
M-estimation and sandwich uncertainty connect robust fitting with asymptotic inference.
Inverting coefficient tests gives matching confidence intervals.
A one-degree-of-freedom Gaussian linear-model comparison has F equal to the matching t statistic squared.
Genome-wide comparisons need a stated error-rate control strategy.
Repeated selection and reuse of data affect inferential claims as well as prediction estimates.
Posterior expectations define the quantities that MCMC approximates.
Intractable posterior integrals motivate deterministic approximations.
Certain MAP objectives match penalties; full posterior inference retains uncertainty beyond the optimum.
Gaussian-prior shrinkage connects ridge-style penalties with partial-pooling models.
Group-level latent effects connect hierarchical Bayes and mixed-effects models.
Both assess predictive behavior beyond the observations used to fit a model.
ANOVA and contrasts can be expressed as linear-model comparisons.
Diagnostics reveal influential observations and motivate sensitivity analyses.
Logistic and Poisson regression instantiate GLMs for different response distributions.
Clustering affects dependence and uncertainty; model-based and sampling-design routes differ.
Smoothing and basis methods connect flexible regression to predictive learning.
Randomization supports treatment exchangeability under the study design.
Randomization can justify permutation reference distributions; arbitrary shuffling cannot.
Both use weights, but inclusion probabilities and treatment propensities answer different questions.
Selection and missingness assumptions determine what observed data can identify.
Kernel weighting is shared by density estimation and local prediction.
Bootstrap inference uses a fitted or empirical law as a simulation model.
Both resample data, but uncertainty estimation and generalization assessment have different targets.
PCA can be computed using an SVD of an appropriately centered data matrix.
Linear variance-preserving summaries contrast with nonlinear neighborhood displays.
Discriminant analysis is a model-based approach to supervised classification.
Temporal modeling uses stochastic-process notions such as stationarity and covariance.
Forecast evaluation preserves time order rather than training on the future.
Hidden Markov models are structured graphical latent-state models.
Event-time regression models time-to-outcome data in clinical studies.
Censoring and missing data both require explicit observation-process assumptions.
Gaussian process regression and kriging share conditional Gaussian prediction.
EM integrates missing or latent quantities in its expectation step.
Random-effects synthesis models study-specific effects within a hierarchy.
Honest reporting requires separating model selection from final evaluation.
Data definitions and joins must preserve the intended units and target population.
Residual and influence displays reveal model failures and unusual observations.
Documented RNG streams and repeatable code make simulation studies auditable.
Automatic differentiation computes gradients used in neural training.
QR or SVD solve regression problems more stably than explicitly inverting a Gram matrix.
Coordinate and proximal methods solve common penalized objectives.
VI turns approximate posterior fitting into an optimization problem.
Both involve density ratios; the log-expectation distinction leads to Jensen's bound.
Computation diagnostics and model criticism examine different possible failures.
EM is a common fitting algorithm for finite mixture models.
Variational autoencoders train a latent-variable model with an ELBO objective.
Ensemble complexity and tuning must be evaluated on appropriate held-out data.
Aggregate predictive accuracy can hide poor subgroup performance.
Exchangeability-based conformal guarantees use a different route from asymptotic normal intervals.
Expected log likelihood and KL relate model fit to distributional discrepancy.
Entropy-based criteria can be used to select classification-tree splits.
